blocks.content: The High Court is the highest judicial authority at the state level in India. It functions under Part VI, Chapter V of the Constitution of India. The provisions regarding High Courts are mainly contained in Articles 214–231.
1. Constitutional Articles Related to High Courts

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Part VI of the Constitution (Articles 214 to 231) deals with the organization, independence, jurisdiction, powers, and procedures of High Courts.
High Court judges are appointed by the President of India after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the state concerned.
To be appointed as a High Court judge, a person must be a citizen of India and have held a judicial office or practiced as an advocate in a High Court for at least 10 years.
Under Article 226, the High Court has the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other legal purpose.
Parliament has the power to establish a common High Court for two or more states or for two or more states and a Union Territory.

blocks.content: 2. Composition of High Court
• A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other judges.
• The number of judges is decided by the President depending on workload.
3. Appointment of High Court Judges
• Judges are appointed by the President of India.
Every High Court shall consist of a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President may from time to time deem it necessary to appoint.
• Consultation with Chief Justice of India, Governor, and Chief Justice of High Court.
4. Qualifications of High Court Judges
• Citizen of India.
• 10 years judicial office OR 10 years advocate in High Court.
5. Tenure

blocks.content: • Judges retire at age 62.
• They can resign to the President.
• They can be removed through impeachment.
6. Jurisdiction of High Court
Original, Appellate, Writ, and Supervisory jurisdiction.
7. Types of Writs

items: The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32, as High Courts can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
High Court judges are appointed by the President of India, but they take their oath or affirmation before the Governor of the respective state.
The retirement age of High Court judges was increased from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963.
Salaries and allowances of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, whereas their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

blocks.content: EXAM Important Facts
• Articles 214–231 deal with High Courts.
• Judges retire at 62.
• High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
